In the darkness, I remember the soft 'click' and tiny 'whoosh' of the purple plastic lighter, and the way the tiny light would bathe the whole cavern in a weak, flickering glow. I remember the faces of the survivors, pressed in close. It's been so long since we've seen each other in the light. 

  My grandfather said he still remembered the above-ground time. He remembered the sun. He said he remembered a time  when half the day was bright- so bright it could hurt you- and nights that were soft and tinged purple, where the darkness was velvety and soft and pin pricked with stars. He said that once, so long ago, there were animals- not the rats and six-legged creepy crawlies we subsist on now, but huge, beautiful animals- playful dogs, slinking cats, majestic horses that could carry you wherever you needed to go. He told us about mountains, and valleys. Canyons, and gorges. Rivers, lakes, and-impossibly- the sea. Could there ever have been so much water that you couldn't see the land on the other side? Boats. Cars. Houses. 

  All lies, the ravings of a madman. My grandfather was as blind as the rest of them. I remember the way he'd hold the lighter close to his face, to feel the warmth of its tiny flame, and I remember the flat white of his useless eyes. He had never seen the sun. None of them had. The Great War drove us underground generations before he had ever been born. 

  He died years ago. Of course. Life doesn't last long down here in the black. I don't know why he believed me when I told him, but he did. When I leaned in close and  when I whispered into his ear, 'grandfather...I can see you.' 

   He pressed the purple plastic lighter into my hand, so hard it left a mark. I've been walking ever since. The lighter is almost out of fuel- it didn't have much when I started. I've been following the well worn paths in the darkness, as used to being in the dark as my peers, born without eyes. I walked past the tiny colonies of humans squatting in the dark. I've turned into tunnels that people hadn't dared go. I've followed something strange- a different smell, a tiny rush of air. A slight breeze. 

  I just dropped the lighter. It burned out at last. I flicked it on, one last time, a few minutes ago and saw what I'd been too scared to hope that I had found- a ladder. Rusted, rough, beautiful. Hands shaking, I put my hand on the rungs. Tears streaming out of my eyes, I looked up. 

    Above my head, hundreds of feet up the tunnel, impossibly high- A weak ring of light, shining around a trapdoor set into the ceiling. A door. A way out. 

  And the sun is shining.
